analysis.one_liner: Makes it a crime for companies and executives to hide known serious product dangers from regulators, workers, and the public.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in late November 2022, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and died there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, for a company or its responsible executives to knowingly sit on knowledge of a serious danger from their products or services. Within 24 hours of learning of such a danger, they would have to tell the federal agency with jurisdiction, then warn affected workers and any identifiable members of the public. It would also make it illegal to fire or retaliate against employees who blow the whistle, and it would void arbitration clauses and waivers covering those claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and consumers who could be hurt by dangerous products or services, because companies would have to warn them quickly instead of staying silent. Whistleblower employees would get new protections against being fired, with reinstatement, back pay, and attorney fees if they win, and they could not be forced into arbitration over these claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers near hidden dangers

how_it_helps.text: Requires a company and its responsible officers to verbally notify the appropriate federal agency of a serious danger within 24 hours of learning of it, and in writing within 15 days, and to warn affected employees and identifiable members of the public as soon as practicable [S3].
Makes knowingly failing to inform and warn a crime punishable by a fine, up to 5 years imprisonment, or both — and bars companies from paying an individual executive's fine on their behalf [S3].

Gives employees who are retaliated against for reporting a serious danger the right to seek reinstatement, back pay with interest, and attorney fees, with a jury trial right and a path to court if the Labor Department does not decide within 180 days [S3].
Bars companies from using predispute arbitration agreements or employment waivers to strip workers of these retaliation protections [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Product manufacturers, consumer-facing service companies, and the corporate officers personally liable under the bill. They would face criminal exposure of up to five years for failing to report, and the operational cost of rapid disclosure whenever a serious danger surfaces.
analysis.who_pays_short: Manufacturers, service companies, and their executives

drawbacks.text: The 24-hour verbal reporting clock applies to any 'serious danger' not readily apparent, which would push companies to report aggressively and could flood federal agencies with marginal warnings, slowing attention to genuinely urgent hazards [S3].

The definition of 'responsible corporate officer' reaches employers, directors, and officers with authority and responsibility over the relevant product or practice, exposing executives to personal criminal liability for reporting failures they may not have personally handled [S3].

The whistleblower provision voids arbitration and waiver agreements for these claims, overriding private employment contracts, which businesses argue removes a dispute forum they negotiated in good faith [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-safety gain is large: people exposed to a hidden danger would learn about it within days, and executives would face prison rather than absorbing silence as a business cost. The costs are real but ordinary for criminal-disclosure regimes — compliance burden, over-reporting risk, and executive liability that may sweep in managers with limited hands-on knowledge. The chief design question is whether the 24-hour standard is workable, not whether disclosure should be mandatory.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on November 29, 2022, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up; five weeks later the Congress ended and the bill died.

narrative.text: Sen. Blumenthal introduced the Hide No Harm Act of 2022 in the Senate on November 29, 2022, joined by Sen. Casey [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
The bill had one cosponsor, Sen. Casey of Pennsylvania [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that make or sell products and services: they keep the ability to handle internally any serious dangers they discover, with no 24-hour reporting clock, no personal criminal liability for executives, and no new anti-retaliation rights for whistleblowing employees.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that never faced a vote

sides.party_line_note: No one ever voted on the bill, and no senator publicly opposed it; the record shows only two Democratic sponsors and no committee action, so no partisan split was ever measured.

industries.industry: Product manufacturers (consumer goods, equipment, and components)
industries.note: The bill would require them to report any serious product danger to a federal agency within 24 hours and warn exposed workers and identifiable members of the public, with criminal penalties for knowing silence. Today such dangers can be handled internally without public warning, which is precisely what the bill is designed to end.

Covered services in interstate commerce fall under the same reporting and warning mandate, so service businesses would owe the same 24-hour agency disclosure and 15-day written report when they learn of a serious danger to customers or workers.

Executives with authority over a dangerous product would face personal criminal liability of up to five years, and the bill bars the company from paying their fine for them, putting their own money and liberty on the line for non-disclosure.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and employers using arbitration clauses
industries.note: The bill voids predispute arbitration agreements for whistleblower retaliation claims under it, removing a forum those employment contracts currently channel such disputes into.
